title: Peasants Going to Work
medium: Etching in brown ink on laid paper; seventh state of seven

image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1924
image.license: Public domain. Released under Creative Commons Zero (CC0) through the Met's Open Access program

altText: A brown-ink etching of country people, a man and a woman, walking out together to their work, drawn with fine, crisscrossing lines.

source.verifiedBy: Met Collection API object record: title, artist, date, medium, public-domain flag, credit line, tags (Men, Women), classification (Prints) and image URLs read from the record; the record gives no country, so France rests on Millet's well-established nationality

context: An etching in brown ink made in 1863 by Jean-François Millet, a French artist known for scenes of rural labor. The Met's record describes this impression as the seventh and final state of the plate.

descriptions.k: Two people walk to work in the countryside. This picture is not made with paint. It is made with lots of tiny lines in brown ink. Can you find the people? Where do you think they are going?
descriptions.g12: Jean-François Millet made this print in France. It shows country people walking out to do their work. The picture is made of many tiny brown lines. Look closely at how lines make shadows and shapes. What kind of work do you think they are going to do?
descriptions.g35: Millet was a French artist who made art about the lives of farm workers. This is an etching: the artist scratched lines into a metal plate, covered it in ink, and pressed it on paper. The brown ink and fine lines show people heading out to work. Look at how the lines create dark and light. Why might Millet show the walk to work, not the work itself?
descriptions.g68: In 1863, Millet made this etching of country people on their way to labor. An etching builds images from lines scratched into a plate, so the artist controls tone through the density of those lines. The brown ink gives a warm, earthy feel. Millet is known for treating rural work with dignity. How does choosing the walk to work, a moment between tasks, shape the way we see these people?
descriptions.g910: Peasants Going to Work shows how Millet used the economy of etching, with crosshatching and varied line, to create tone and mood without color. Choosing a moment of passage rather than of labor itself keeps the focus on routine and endurance. Critics in the 1800s debated whether his rural subjects honored workers or unsettled urban viewers. How does the medium's restraint affect your reading, and what does the title ask you to assume?
descriptions.g1112: Millet's etching belongs to a body of work that brought rural labor into serious art in nineteenth-century France, and it was received in sharply different ways: as respectful, as sentimental, or as politically unsettling. The medium itself matters. Line density builds tone, and an impression described as a final state shows how an image is refined over time. How do medium, subject and the viewpoint of a buyer shape what this print can claim to show?

g1112.color: How does the monochrome ink shape the print's reception, and how might the paper's age affect what we see?
g1112.texture: How does a purely linear medium suggest material difference, and what limits does it impose?
g1112.space: How does the print negotiate depth and flatness within the conventions of etching?
g1112.light: In what ways does the interplay of paper and ink function as both description of light and a device of mood?

teacherNote.context: Millet made paintings, drawings and etchings of French rural labor. An etching is made by scratching lines into a coated metal plate, which is then inked and pressed on paper.
directions: Have students make a small drawing using only line, building dark and light with hatching.
Ask students to write what happens next, then discuss which visual evidence they used.
Compare with a colorful work from the archive and discuss what color adds or removes.
